produces: Graded, hyperbolic (Michaelian) response; exponential approach to equilibrium; switching on is faster than switching off
needs: Ligand in large excess over receptor
molecules: β2-adrenergic receptor, epinephrine
comment: Halftime falls with faster association and with faster dissociation. The off time is set by the dissociation rate alone (complex half-life).

pattern: Binding and activation as separate steps
produces: Basal activity and incomplete maximal activity; explains full agonists, partial agonists, antagonists, inverse agonists
needs: Receptor with inactive and active conformations
molecules: µ-opioid receptor; morphine, heroin, fentanyl; naloxone
comment: Drug classes differ in how strongly they favour the active conformation, not only in affinity.

produces: Sigmoidal, switch-like (ultrasensitive) binding
needs: Multimeric receptor; binding of the first ligand favours the next (Hill, MWC or KNF models)
molecules: Haemoglobin, O2
comment: Hill exponent 2.7 for haemoglobin with 4 sites. Load in lungs, unload in tissues.

produces: Response flatter than Michaelian; works over a wider ligand range without saturating
needs: First binding lowers affinity of the second site (KNF model; MWC cannot fit it)
molecules: Drosophila EGFR, Spitz; insulin receptor
comment: Hill exponent 0.24 for Spitz on EGFR, 0.46 for insulin.

produces: Sharp threshold in activation
needs: High-affinity ligand in limited supply; first site acts as a buffer that must fill before the activating site
molecules: EGFR, EGF, TGFα
comment: When the upstream regulator is depleted by binding (usual inside cells), the response becomes more linear than hyperbolic.

produces: Threshold, then switch-like rise of the output
needs: High-affinity inhibitor present below the activator; activator must titrate it out first
example: Opioid antagonism; Drosophila EGFR; cell cycle
molecules: Naloxone vs heroin at µ-opioid receptor; Argos sequesters Spitz; CDK inhibitors p21Cip1, p27Kip1, p16INK4a, p19INK4a on cyclin–Cdk
comment: A common way to build ultrasensitivity from plain binding.

produces: Michaelian steady state; exponential approach
needs: Opposing enzymes working far from saturation (mass action)
molecules: Any kinase/phosphatase pair
comment: System reaches a steady state, not an equilibrium. Rate-balance plots read the steady states and dynamics.

produces: Very switch-like steady state
needs: Kinase and phosphatase near saturation (substrate above their KM; Goldbeter–Koshland)
molecules: Glycogen phosphorylase, phosphorylase kinase, phosphorylase phosphatase
comment: Sigmoidal at 70 µM substrate, not at 20 µM. Phosphorylase reaches about 100 µM in muscle, so it may apply in vivo.

produces: Ultrasensitive steady state (KNF-like); lag in activation
needs: Two or more sites needed for activity (AND logic), distributive phosphorylation
molecules: ERK2 phosphorylated on Thr and Tyr by MEK
comment: The shape of the activation time course tells the number of rate-limiting steps.

produces: Positive cooperativity in multisite phosphorylation
needs: First phosphorylation creates a docking site that recruits the kinase for the next sites
example: Cell cycle Cdk substrates; GSK3 and CK1 substrates
molecules: Cyclin–Cdk–Cks (Cks binds phosphothreonine); GSK3; CK1
comment: Works in disordered regions, where allostery is unlikely: proximity in place of conformation change.

produces: Sharper discrimination of on-target over off-target substrates
needs: Distributive phosphorylation of several sites, each with a chance of reversal
example: Parallel MAPK cascades with little cross-talk
molecules: Raf/Mos, MEK1/2, ERK1/2; JNKKKs, MKK4/7, JNK1 to 3; p38 cascade
comment: Specificity of each step multiplies.

produces: Extra ultrasensitivity from sites that are not needed for activity
needs: Sites that compete for the kinase or ligand without being required
molecules: MEK1 (fully active after the first phosphorylation); nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (pentamer)

produces: Ultrasensitivity
needs: Input activates the forward enzyme and inhibits the reverse one
molecules: DNA damage activates Wee1 and inhibits Cdc25; both act on cyclin B–Cdk1
comment: Same algebra as the KNF equation.

produces: Linear steady state; halftime set by the destruction rate only
needs: Synthesis driven by input, first-order destruction
molecules: Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase, ATP to cAMP, cAMP activates PKA and cAMP-gated channels; opsin, transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase, cGMP-gated Na+ channels close
comment: A modification cycle returns to steady state faster than a synthesis–destruction system with the same flux.

produces: Threshold; output runs away when synthesis exceeds maximal destruction
needs: Destruction enzyme near saturation
molecules: Phenytoin (zero-order elimination) vs carbamazepine (first-order)
comment: A 50% higher phenytoin dose can give toxic levels.

produces: Large downstream output reached fast from few active upstream molecules
needs: Each tier an enzyme that activates many of the next
molecules: Raf, MEK, ERK; retina detecting few photons; immune system detecting few peptide antigens
comment: A 3-tier cascade does in under 30 s what one kinase would need about 17 min for (book's estimate).

produces: Ultrasensitivity multiplies down the cascade; graded responses get more graded
needs: Tiers in series; sensitivities multiply
molecules: Mos, MEK1, ERK2 (Hill 1.7 for MEK1, 5 for ERK2)

produces: Ultrasensitive response
needs: Input reaches the output by two routes with the same sign
example: Arabinose use; PKC activation; Akt activation
molecules: CRP–cAMP drives araC and araBAD/araFGH, AraC–arabinose also drives araBAD/araFGH; PLC makes DAG and IP3, IP3 releases Ca2+, DAG and Ca2+ together activate PKC; PIP3 activates Akt directly and through PDK1
comment: The book also counts oligomeric receptors and multisite phosphorylation as variations of this motif.

produces: Pulse and perfect adaptation
needs: Input acts on the target through an activator and, later, an inhibitor
molecules: EGFR recruits Sos (through Shc, Grb2) then p120 RasGAP; also RasGRP and Shp-1 on Ras
comment: Strict ordering of Sos then GAP binding is not required.

produces: All-or-none, irreversible or hysteretic response; memory of a transient input
needs: Feedback plus nonlinearity (ultrasensitivity) plus balanced rates; saddle-node bifurcation
molecules: Progesterone, Mos, MEK, ERK2 (ERK2 drives Mos synthesis), Cdk1
comment: Blocking Mos translation makes the response graded. Cell fate decisions in general are described as all-or-none and irreversible.

produces: Switching on needs more input than staying on; reversible
needs: Weaker positive feedback than the irreversible case
molecules: Cyclin B–Cdk1

pattern: Two-variable positive or double-negative feedback (toggle switch)
produces: Bistability with two stable states and a saddle
needs: Mutual activation, or mutual inhibition with ultrasensitivity
molecules: Cdk1 inhibits Wee1 and Wee1 inhibits Cdk1; generic pair of repressors
comment: A perfectly symmetric pair gives a pitchfork bifurcation; small asymmetry turns it into a saddle-node.

produces: Critical point: below it nothing happens, above it explosive growth or a new phase; sigmoidal time course
needs: Self-reinforcing uptake or spread
molecules: P granules, nucleoli, centrosomes, heterochromatin; phospholipid vesicles; SARS-CoV-2 (SIR model, R0)
organism: C. elegans embryo; in vitro; human population
comment: Critical concentration xcrit equals k−1/k1; epidemic grows if R0·S0 is above 1.

produces: Steady state more stable; faster approach to it
needs: Output inhibits its own producer
example: Second messenger or protein that inhibits its own production
molecules: Generic (product binds its producing enzyme or mRNA)
comment: Gives a faster response without a pulse.

pattern: Long positive feedback through ligand shedding
produces: Reinforces and spreads EGFR activity to neighbouring cells
needs: Sheddase activated downstream of the receptor
molecules: EGFR, ADAM17, TGFα (PKC likely intermediate)
comment: How ADAM17 is activated is not worked out (book).

produces: Self-reinforcing Ras activation
needs: Product binds and activates its own activator
molecules: Ras-GTP binds Sos allosterically

produces: Pulse, then return to baseline under constant input; perfect when the feedback reactions are saturated
needs: Feedback with delay; saturation or high ultrasensitivity in the loop for perfect adaptation
molecules: Tar (aspartate), Tsr (serine) receptors, CheW, CheA, CheY, CheR methylation, CheB demethylation
comment: Adaptation stays perfect when protein levels change (robust, Barkai–Leibler).

produces: Transient ERK activity under sustained mitogen
needs: Induction of a phosphatase by the pathway output
molecules: ERK2 induces MKP1/DUSP1; ERK also inhibits Sos, Raf, MEK, EGFR
comment: Blocking new gene products does not stop the ERK pulse in PC12, 3T3-L1 and PAE cells, so other loops act there. KRas G12V gives prolonged signalling in cancer.

produces: Pulse and perfect adaptation through closed, open, inactivated states
needs: Active form converted to a third, inactive state
example: Action potential; receptor internalization; GPCR desensitisation
molecules: Voltage-gated Na+ channel; EGFR internalization; β2-adrenergic receptor phosphorylated by βARK, then β-arrestin binding switches signalling from G protein to ERK; µ-opioid receptor
organism: Nerve and heart; mammalian cells; mice
comment: Biased opioid agonists: G protein mediates analgesia, β-arrestin respiratory depression and addiction (mouse data).

produces: Sustained limit-cycle oscillations
needs: At least 3 steps in the loop and strong ultrasensitivity (Hill above 8); Hopf bifurcation
example: Model used for circadian clocks and myxobacteria gliding
molecules: mRNA, enzyme, product that represses the gene (generic)
comment: Two-variable negative feedback gives only pulses or damped oscillations.

pattern: Relaxation oscillator: negative feedback plus bistable trigger
produces: Spikes of activity; period tunable with little change in amplitude
needs: Fast bistable switch, slow negative feedback
molecules: Cyclin B synthesis; Cdk1; Cdc25 (positive feedback); Wee1 (double-negative feedback); APC/C–Cdc20 destroys cyclin B (negative feedback); Greatwall, ENSA, ARPP19 inhibit PP2A-B55
comment: Hill exponent at least 17 for Cdk1 on APC/C–Cdc20 (Table 5.1).

pattern: Interlinked fast and slow positive feedback loops
produces: More all-or-none and more robust trigger
needs: Two loops on different time scales
molecules: Cdk1–Cdc25 and Cdk1–Wee1

produces: Periodic electrical spikes
needs: Fast voltage switch, slow recovery variable
molecules: Membrane voltage, ion channels
comment: Same logic as the cell cycle oscillator, from ions in place of proteins.

pattern: Depletion in place of negative feedback
produces: Pulsatile oscillations
needs: Three-state activation cycle with positive feedback; recovery by depletion of the inactive pool
molecules: RhoA (cytoplasmic GDP form, membrane GDP form, GTP form), GEF

produces: Irregular spikes when noise pushes past a threshold; input raises spike frequency
needs: Fast positive feedback, slow negative feedback, steady state close to a Hopf bifurcation
molecules: ERK activates metalloproteases that release EGF and TGFα onto EGFR (positive); MKP induction (negative). Other candidate loops: EGFR–phosphatases, Ras-GTP activates Sos, ERK dual phosphorylation, FGF release
comment: Noise is part of the mechanism, not a disturbance. The book chose the metalloprotease loop for its model, not from proof.
